name: Albendazole
route_note: single chewable 400 mg dose for intestinal worms; twice daily with a fatty meal for tissue infections such as neurocysticercosis and hydatid disease
originator: SmithKline Animal Health (Robert Gyurik and Vassilios Theodorides)
owner: generic (many); GSK (Zentel, donated for mass drug administration)

discovery.by: Robert J. Gyurik and Vassilios J. Theodorides, SmithKline
discovery.note: Broad-spectrum benzimidazole carbamate first developed as a veterinary anthelmintic.

tagline: Single-dose deworming tablet given to hundreds of millions of children each year
summary: Albendazole is a broad-spectrum benzimidazole anthelmintic that binds worm tubulin and blocks glucose uptake. A single dose treats common intestinal worms and is used in school-based deworming and lymphatic filariasis elimination programmes worldwide, supported by GSK donations. Longer courses treat tissue infections such as neurocysticercosis and hydatid disease.
mechanism: Albendazole is converted in the liver to albendazole sulfoxide, the main active metabolite. It binds the colchicine-sensitive site of helminth β-tubulin and prevents polymerisation into microtubules.

Loss of cytoplasmic microtubules impairs glucose uptake and transport of secretory vesicles in intestinal cells of the worm, depleting glycogen and ATP and leading to immobilisation and death. It binds parasite tubulin far more strongly than mammalian tubulin.
uses: Soil-transmitted helminths (roundworm, hookworm, whipworm) and pinworm
Lymphatic filariasis (with ivermectin or diethylcarbamazine in mass drug administration)
Giardiasis, strongyloidiasis and cutaneous larva migrans (some regimens)

history.title: Discovery
history.detail: Albendazole is discovered at SmithKline Animal Health in Philadelphia.

history.title: Human use
history.detail: Albendazole is introduced for human use (Zentel).

history.title: FDA approval
history.detail: Albenza is approved in the US for neurocysticercosis and hydatid disease.

history.title: Donation programme
history.detail: SmithKline Beecham (later GSK) commits to donate albendazole for the Global Programme to Eliminate Lymphatic Filariasis, later expanded to school deworming.

history.title: Triple therapy
history.detail: WHO recommends ivermectin, diethylcarbamazine and albendazole (IDA) for lymphatic filariasis in selected settings.

pk.bioavailability: poor (under 5%), increased up to fivefold with a fatty meal
pk.metabolism: rapid first-pass oxidation to albendazole sulfoxide (active), then to the sulfone
pk.excretion: mainly biliary; small amounts in urine

serious: neurological symptoms from dying cysts in neurocysticercosis (seizures, raised intracranial pressure)

facts: GSK has donated billions of albendazole tablets for neglected tropical disease programmes.
In the US, the price of albendazole rose sharply in the 2010s, illustrating the high cost of old drugs with few suppliers.
